extracted.intended_audience: university-level public relations instructors and communication department curriculum planners
extracted.subtask_description: A pedagogical model for integrating word-processing/computer technology into undergraduate public relations writing courses to improve writing process, creativity, management skills, and job-market readiness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Objective One: To make the computer disappear as a machine
rubrics_metrics.description: To make the computer disappear as a machine (e.g., one does not need to know about carburetors to drive a car; similarly, one does not need to know about baud and bytes to effectively utilize computers).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teach only the operational essentials needed to use the computer as a writing tool; avoid exposing students to unnecessary technical detail that distracts from writing. Use analogies (monitor as TV screen, keyboard as typewriter, disk as paper files) to reduce intimidation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Objective Two: View the computer as another writing tool
rubrics_metrics.description: The computer is viewed as a tool like one's typewriter or pencil; develop a sense of the computer as essential and indispensable for varied conditions and highlight capabilities beyond pencil/typewriter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasize tangible advantages (capabilities that could never be accomplished with pencil/typewriter), but keep focus on tool-use for writing rather than on learning computer science.

rubrics_metrics.name: Objective Three: Use the computer as a management tool
rubrics_metrics.description: The computer is utilized as a management tool which supports, enhances, and improves one's writing output (editing, time limits, rewrites, simulating team efforts like peer editing and multiple versions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design assignments that require versioning, peer/instructor review, deadline-driven rewrites, and shared documents so students practice real-world PR management tasks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Objective Four: Enhance classroom creativity
rubrics_metrics.description: The computer is utilized in a way that enhances more creativity in the classroom: it flows as fast as students' thoughts, assists editing, and provides instant feedback, freeing students to explore and reach new levels of creativity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use brainstorming and free-writing exercises on the computer to de-emphasize final-form concerns and encourage idea generation; stress 'keep fingers moving' to stimulate thought.

rubrics_metrics.name: Training philosophy: applied, non-cognitive, context-driven learning
rubrics_metrics.description: Adopt a Heidegger/Winograd & Flores-influenced orientation: knowing is never complete, applied knowledge is more fundamental than theory, cognitive labeling isn't primary, and learning is social rather than purely individual.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor 'skills for doing' over theoretical lectures; introduce new material only when a student encounters a contextual need ('breakdown') to avoid information overload; let students create contexts that motivate learning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Laboratory access and configuration requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Communication departments should have access to computer laboratories where each student has a computer available and the lab has copies of the required software at each station.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure labs are sized to class enrollment (example: 28-student limit), stocked with multiple copies of word processing software, and open for out-of-class work; university technical resources should be shared with communication departments if possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Instructional focus: teach the computer as tool, not computer science
rubrics_metrics.description: Instruction should be focused on the computer as a tool for writing rather than on computer science topics; requiring a computer science course may defeat the communication student's needs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide minimal, targeted training (e.g., two 90-minute lab sessions early in the semester), offer a two-page step-by-step on essentials (formatting, opening/saving/printing/exiting), and supply keyboard reference grids to avoid overwhelming students.

rubrics_metrics.name: Immediate, action-based initial training
rubrics_metrics.description: Initial training requires immediate word-processing action rather than 'how-to' lectures; turn-on-and-do activities demystify computers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use hands-on activities during the first lab sessions so students perform basic tasks (create, save, print) and learn new features only as needs arise; avoid assigning software manuals as mandatory reading.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use brainstorming assignments to familiarize students and stimulate idea flow
rubrics_metrics.description: Enable brainstorming sessions on the computer to de-emphasize final writing and allow students to type as fast as they think, reducing concern about details and encouraging idea pushing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Schedule multiple brainstorming sessions, ask students to keep fingers moving, and have instructors respond to breakdowns in usage; use the computer's speed to bypass handwriting legibility and other practical barriers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide at least one supervised lab experience for all students
rubrics_metrics.description: Assure that each student has at least one supervised experience on the computer with word-processing software so novices can gain comfort and learn basic options.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow supervised sessions with open-lab access and lab consultants for additional practice; allow more experienced students to explore advanced keyboard options under supervision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Introduce short, simple assignments to teach peer review and editing workflows
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a very short and simple news-release assignment to introduce multiple copies for peer and instructor review and editing; store drafts in directories for rewrite.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make editing collaborative by having at least three reviewers per draft; emphasize that editing is easier and more interactive when not handwritten.

rubrics_metrics.name: Develop students' management skills through task sequencing
rubrics_metrics.description: Students should experience being in charge of initial creation, printing, contacting editors/distributing copies, rewriting, and assessing development—made easier by computers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design assignments and class processes that require students to manage each stage of a PR writing project to simulate professional workflows.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enable higher assignment throughput and iterative feedback
rubrics_metrics.description: Computers allow students to complete more assignments under time limitations and receive more feedback, leading to fuller completion and more practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exploit speed and ease of revision to assign multiple drafts and provide iterative instructor/peer feedback within constrained class times.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain logs and 'to do' lists for project tracking
rubrics_metrics.description: Students should easily update goals/objectives and provide weekly 'log of activities' that can be shared with classmates or teams.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Incorporate weekly logs as part of coursework to encourage reflection, accountability, and team coordination; use shared files or directories for transparency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teach revising for multiple PR formats from a single idea
rubrics_metrics.description: Students should be able to revise a writing assignment into a variety of formats (pitch letter, news feature, broadcast announcement), e.g., designing PSA versions of 10, 30, and 60 seconds by duplicating and editing the core idea.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assign tasks requiring format adaptation; show how duplication + targeted editing produces different-length broadcast spots and messages for varied audiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Encourage production of multiple copies for teams and stakeholders
rubrics_metrics.description: The computer should facilitate producing multiple copies of progress reports, final reports, and other materials for team members, clients, and instructors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Build team-based assignments that rely on easy duplication and distribution of drafts to foster collaborative editing and client-style workflows.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use spelling-checker and red-flag dictionaries to build accuracy
rubrics_metrics.description: Students should use built-in spelling checkers and create personal 'red-flag' dictionaries of words they frequently misspell.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teach students to use and maintain custom dictionaries to address recurring errors (which may be faulty typing habits), improving polish and reducing simple proofreading issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Staff open computing laboratories with professional consultants
rubrics_metrics.description: Writing assignments should be completed in open computing laboratories staffed with professional consultants who can assist with hardware/software breakdowns and student questions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure consultants are oriented to word-processing support for liberal-arts students (not highly technical-only staff); have consultants available during peak assignment times.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid information overload by introducing features on demand
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid overwhelming students with irrelevant information; present new material when students ask or encounter a contextual need (the 'breakdown').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Differentiate between knowledge needed for task completion and deeper technical learning; let students seek information pertinent to their immediate needs to keep motivation high.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide accommodations for access issues and breakdowns
rubrics_metrics.description: Allow alternative completion methods (e.g., typewriter) when students have legitimate access hardships, commute constraints, or experience data loss from failures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accept occasional non-computer submissions if campus access or reliability issues interfere, while making clear that the course sequence will continue to use computer technology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessment of success: student evaluations and employment outcomes
rubrics_metrics.description: Measure model success via student evaluations (e.g., high ratings, positive open-ended comments), internship/performance reports from agencies and corporations, and increased hiring due to students' computer experience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Collect standardized and open-ended feedback; track internship/professional placement outcomes and employer comments about professionalism and technical readiness as indicators of program effectiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Curriculum integration recommendation (tool-focused)
rubrics_metrics.description: Integrate computer experiences into the public relations curriculum as applied tool-training embedded in PR courses rather than by requiring separate computer science courses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argue to departments that applied, tool-based computer instruction is more relevant to PR students; recommend sharing technical resources across departments to implement labs and training.
